title: Automated Discovery of Physically Interpretable Subgrid Length Scales for Detached Eddy Simulation via Agentic AI
authors: Jiawei Chen, Xiang I. A. Yang, Ping He
abstract: Traditional turbulence-model development relies heavily on expert knowledge and is time-consuming. This study develops an agentic AI framework, DEScover (automated Discovery of DES closures), to explore subgrid length scales for detached eddy simulation (DES). The user provides only a modeling idea: the length scale is the grid width normal to the local vortex axis. Four large language model (LLM) agents then propose, review, implement, and evaluate candidate formulations and generate scripts for CFD simulations. The Discovery Agent infers the vortex axis from various vortex-identification methods. The candidates are tested on four cases spanning canonical and engineering flows: a flat plate, a backward-facing step, a free shear layer, and an iced airfoil. For all test cases, the best candidate consistently outperforms the standard length scale based on the maximum cell size. Its accuracy is similar to, or slightly better than, that of the expert-designed shear-layer-adapted length scale. Each agentic discovery run takes about 25 minutes on average, excluding the CFD simulations. These results show that LLM-based reasoning can significantly accelerate the discovery of physically interpretable turbulence models and reduce reliance on manual expert formulation.

infographic.key_insight: DEScover uses four LLM agents to discover physically interpretable DES subgrid length scales from the idea of measuring grid width normal to the local vortex axis.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could accelerate turbulence-model development while reducing reliance on manual expert formulation.
method: Infer local vortex axes using different vortex-identification methods.
Use four agents to propose, review, implement, and evaluate candidate length scales.
Generate CFD simulation scripts to test candidate formulations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across a flat plate, backward-facing step, free shear layer, and iced airfoil, the best candidate consistently outperformed the maximum-cell-size baseline and matched or slightly exceeded an expert-designed shear-layer-adapted scale.
infographic.watch_item: The reported average discovery time of about 25 minutes excludes CFD simulations, and broader generalization beyond the four test cases remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Automated Discovery of Physically Interpretable Subgrid Length Scales for Detached Eddy Simulation via Agentic AI

title: A Priori Estimation of the Non-Linear Compression Potential and Quantification of Autoencoder Non-Linearity in Turbulent Flows
authors: Niklas Alexander Pissarski, Juan Pablo Murcia Leon, Søren Juhl Andersen
abstract: Data-driven reduced-order modelling (ROM) of turbulent flows is based on an efficient and physical low-dimensional representation of the flow process. Such a dimension reduction can be achieved using proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) or non-linear autoencoders. Capturing the inherent non-linearities in turbulent flows offers the potential for improved compression rates. This work proposes the local tangent residual (LTR) as an a priori estimate of the potential benefit of non-linear dimension reduction for a given dataset. The LTR is based on the local geometry of the data points, requiring neither prior model training nor the definition of a threshold parameter. For all datasets investigated in this work, namely, two vortex street cases and the turbulent wake flow of a wind turbine, the dominant trends in autoencoder compression performance are reproduced by the proposed LTR. The results are further contextualised through the decoder linearisation error (DLE). The DLE quantifies the non-linearity of the trained decoder by comparing it to a linearised surrogate model, which enables physical interpretability of the non-linearities. Together, a large non-linear compression potential in the turbulent flow, as quantified by the LTR, is corroborated by a large DLE, i.e., a pronounced non-linearity captured in the trained autoencoder. The LTR thus enables practitioners in turbulent flow modelling to determine a priori whether non-linear compression is worthwhile, avoiding the substantial computational cost of autoencoder architecture search and hyperparameter tuning in cases where POD already suffices.

infographic.key_insight: The local tangent residual (LTR) estimates whether turbulent-flow data could benefit from nonlinear compression before training an autoencoder.
infographic.engineering_relevance: LTR can help practitioners choose between POD and nonlinear autoencoders, potentially avoiding costly architecture searches and hyperparameter tuning when POD suffices.
method: Compute LTR from local data geometry without model training or a threshold parameter.
Compare LTR trends with autoencoder compression performance.
Quantify trained-decoder nonlinearity using decoder linearisation error (DLE) relative to a linearised surrogate.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across two vortex street cases and a turbulent wind-turbine wake, LTR reproduced dominant autoencoder compression trends, while large nonlinear compression potential was corroborated by large DLE.
infographic.watch_item: Validation covers three flow datasets; reliability across broader turbulent regimes and data-sampling conditions remains to be established.
infographic.paper_title: A Priori Estimation of the Non-Linear Compression Potential and Quantification of Autoencoder Non-Linearity in Turbulent Flows

title: Assisted Turbulence Modeling via Data Assimilation and Machine Learning for Turbomachinery Flows
authors: Tom Moussie, Pierric Joseph, Marcello Meldi
abstract: This work presents the development and assessment of a hybrid framework coupling numerical simulation, experimental samples, data assimilation (DA) and machine learning (ML) to investigate the flow within an axial compressor stage. The methodology first implements a Multi-Fidelity Ensemble Kalman Filter (MFEnKF) which integrates experimental PIV data with a two-fidelity numerical simulation setup, combining steady-state RANS on a fixed grid with unsteady hybrid RANS/LES simulations on a moving grid. This data assimilation step successfully reduces discrepancies between experiments and CFD realizations. Besides, it provides additional high fidelity samples when compared with the available PIV data. This enriched database is used to train machine learning (ML) tools, with the objective to obtain black-box forcing terms to be included in the discretized form of the Navier-Stokes equations. These models are expected to preserve the accuracy of the DA results while not longer requiring the input of experimental data. The neural network architecture used here maps local physical features such as the velocity, the velocity gradients and the turbulent viscosity, to obtain the volume forcing terms. The analysis of the performance of such ML models shows that global accuracy is preserved but localized increased errors in specific regions of the compressor, such as close to the blade tips, can exceed those observed from the baseline RANS simulations. To resolve this issue, a Mixture of Experts (MoE) method is employed, which classifies and combines the trained ML tools for different flow regions. The discrepancy with experimental data of this method is systematically lower than the one observed for the baseline RANS solution and very similar to the one obtained with the MFEnKF.

infographic.key_insight: Region-aware Mixture of Experts forcing models achieve compressor-flow accuracy similar to data assimilation without requiring experimental inputs during deployment.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a route to more accurate axial-compressor CFD by learning corrections to baseline turbulence-model predictions.
method: Fuse experimental PIV data with fixed-grid steady RANS and moving-grid hybrid RANS/LES using a Multi-Fidelity Ensemble Kalman Filter.
Train neural networks on the enriched database to map local velocity, velocity gradients and turbulent viscosity to discrete Navier–Stokes forcing terms.
Use a Mixture of Experts to combine learned corrections for different flow regions.
infographic.evidence_signal: In the reported compressor assessment, Mixture of Experts discrepancies from experimental data were systematically lower than baseline RANS and very similar to MFEnKF results.
infographic.watch_item: Individual neural models produced localized errors near blade tips exceeding baseline RANS; generalization beyond the assessed compressor flow remains unestablished in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Assisted Turbulence Modeling via Data Assimilation and Machine Learning for Turbomachinery Flows

title: Synthetic Dataset Generation, Physical Consistency and Active Learning for Shape-Informed Surrogate Modeling of Hemodynamics
authors: Francesco Romor, Richard Schussnig, Charles A. Taylor, Gerhard A. Holzapfel, Alfonso Caiazzo
abstract: Model order reduction has the potential to enable real-time patient-specific assessment of cardiovascular flows. However, it still faces significant challenges stemming from the geometric variability of vascular anatomies. Building upon the SynthAorta dataset (Bosnjak et al., IEEE Trans. Med. Imag. 45(1), 2026) of physiological aortic geometries, we generate an extensive dataset of physiologically consistent computational fluid dynamics solutions through an automatic boundary-condition adjustment procedure. A common reference geometry allows all patient-specific anatomies to be represented by displacement fields, providing point-to-point correspondence without the need for geometric registration. Based on this dataset, we develop Graph U-Net and Transformer U-Net surrogate models to predict velocity and pressure fields at peak systole. We further investigate two strategies to enhance data efficiency and prediction accuracy: active learning and differentiable physical consistency constraints based on the finite element residual. The results show that active learning is strongly regime-dependent: while it offers little benefit over random sampling during early training, it improves performance during fine-tuning through gradient- and subspace-based acquisition strategies. Similarly, physical consistency constraints prove to be substantially more effective as a fine-tuning objective than as a regularizer applied throughout training. Finally, out-of-distribution studies demonstrate that the primary limitation of surrogate models lies in the geometric support of the underlying parametrization rather than in the neural network architectures themselves. The proposed framework combines synthetic dataset generation, geometry-aware surrogate modeling, physics-informed optimization, and active learning into a scalable workflow for inter-patient hemodynamic prediction.

infographic.key_insight: For geometry-aware hemodynamic surrogates, active learning and physics-based constraints work best during fine-tuning, while out-of-distribution performance is primarily limited by geometric coverage.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The workflow supports scalable prediction of patient-specific aortic velocity and pressure fields toward real-time cardiovascular assessment.
method: Generate synthetic aortic CFD solutions with automatically adjusted boundary conditions for physiological consistency.
Represent anatomies as displacement fields from a common reference and train Graph U-Net and Transformer U-Net models at peak systole.
Evaluate active-learning acquisition strategies and differentiable finite-element residual constraints.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluations on the SynthAorta-based CFD dataset show little early-training benefit from active learning, but gains from gradient- and subspace-based acquisition during fine-tuning; physical constraints are also more effective during fine-tuning.
infographic.watch_item: Generalization to unseen anatomies remains constrained by the geometric support of the underlying parametrization.
infographic.paper_title: Synthetic Dataset Generation, Physical Consistency and Active Learning for Shape-Informed Surrogate Modeling of Hemodynamics

title: GeoDiv KAN Solver for Time Fractional Navier Stokes Equations on Complex Domains to Realistic CFD Reconstruction
authors: Yatin Kumar, Shivani Saini, Ramesh Kumar Vats
abstract: Scientific machine learning provides a promising framework for solving complex problems in science and engineering. Notably, physics informed neural networks (PINNs) have shown considerable potential for solving differential equations and modelling engineering systems. Solving time fractional Navier Stokes equations (TFNSEs) on complex domains is challenging due to temporal nonlocality, nonlinear flow dynamics, geometric complexity, and incompressibility constraints. To address these challenges, we propose a geometry gated, divergence-free Gaussian radial basis function Kolmogorov Arnold network (GeoDiv KAN). The proposed architecture uses geometry dependent feature gating and a streamfunction formulation to preserve incompressibility by construction. GeoDiv KAN is evaluated for the time fractional incompressible Navier-Stokes equations on square, circular, and star-shaped domains. Numerical experiments show that GeoDiv KAN achieves higher predictive accuracy than PINN, PIKAN, RBF KAN, and DF RBFKAN across the considered benchmark problems. To establish practical relevance, GeoDiv KAN is applied to two data driven CFD cases: unsteady flow past a circular cylinder using the \href{https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.5039610}{Zenodo dataset} and turbulent RANS flow through a complex U bend using the \href{https://huggingface.co/datasets/JDecke/ubend-cfd}{U-bend dataset}.

infographic.key_insight: GeoDiv KAN combines geometry-dependent feature gating with built-in incompressibility to solve time-fractional Navier–Stokes equations on complex domains.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach targets geometry-aware flow prediction and CFD reconstruction, with applications to unsteady cylinder flow and turbulent U-bend flow.
method: Gaussian radial basis function Kolmogorov–Arnold network.
Geometry-dependent gating adapts features to domain shape.
Streamfunction formulation enforces incompressibility by construction.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports higher predictive accuracy than PINN, PIKAN, RBF KAN, and DF RBFKAN on square, circular, and star-shaped benchmarks, plus applications to public cylinder-flow and U-bend RANS datasets.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no quantitative error or runtime results, leaving accuracy gains and computational scalability to be assessed.
infographic.paper_title: GeoDiv KAN Solver for Time Fractional Navier Stokes Equations on Complex Domains to Realistic CFD Reconstruction

title: A novel machine learning framework based on proper orthogonal decomposition for turbine wake flow predictions in natural waterways
authors: Mustafa Meriç Aksen, Hossein Seyedzadeh, Mehrshad Gholami Anjiraki, Ali Khosronejad
abstract: We developed a machine learning (ML) surrogate trained on instantaneous large eddy simulation (LES) data filtered using proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) to predict mean flow fields in natural rivers with complex geometries. The surrogate enables efficient prediction of mean flow fields downstream of marine hydrokinetic (MHK) turbine arrays at a fraction of the computational cost of high fidelity simulations, facilitating turbine layout optimization in natural waterways where bathymetry, turbulence, and turbine interactions influence the available energy resource. We demonstrate the capabilities of the model at a real world tidal river site under ebb tide conditions. Complex bed bathymetry and planform geometry generate substantial background turbulence that can obscure turbine wake signatures. POD is employed to extract relevant flow structures, improving the ability of the ML model to learn wake dynamics. First, LES is performed at the tidal site to generate training data. POD is then applied to decompose the instantaneous LES fields into spatial modes. Selected modes are used to train a three dimensional convolutional encoder decoder network to predict time averaged velocity fields. This selective filtering reduces the influence of dominant background fluctuations while preserving information relevant to turbine wakes. At equivalent network size and training cost, the POD filtered surrogate reduces the mean squared error by three orders of magnitude compared with the same network trained on unfiltered LES data.

infographic.key_insight: POD filtering helps a machine-learning surrogate distinguish turbine wakes from complex river turbulence, reducing mean squared error by three orders of magnitude versus training on unfiltered LES data.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Fast predictions of mean downstream flow could support marine hydrokinetic turbine layout optimization in natural waterways.
method: Generate instantaneous flow data using large eddy simulation (LES).
Apply proper orthogonal decomposition (POD) and select modes that retain wake-relevant structures.
Train a 3D convolutional encoder–decoder to predict time-averaged velocity fields.
infographic.evidence_signal: At a real-world tidal river site under ebb conditions, the POD-filtered surrogate outperformed the unfiltered-data baseline at equivalent network size and training cost.
infographic.watch_item: Generalization to other sites, tidal conditions, and turbine layouts is not established in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: A novel machine learning framework based on proper orthogonal decomposition for turbine wake flow predictions in natural waterways

title: DiffVortex: A quantum-inspired fast solver for incompressible flows
authors: Yu Jun Loo, Silas Alben, Shravan Veerapaneni
abstract: Matrix-product-state (MPS) and quantized tensor-train (QTT) representations offer a promising framework for computational fluid dynamics, with logarithmic run time and memory scaling in mesh size when bond dimensions remain bounded. Existing MPS-based solvers are Eulerian: they compress velocity fields and enforce immersed-body boundary conditions through static masks or body-fitted coordinates. Moving or flexible bodies complicate this approach: deformation requires updating MPS masks every time step, while filamentary vorticity in high-Reynolds-number flows may resist low-rank compression. We propose a complementary approach: compress the Biot--Savart kernel rather than the flow state, evolve vorticity using Lagrangian vortex particles, and represent immersed bodies by bound vortex sheets on Lagrangian surface points. Our main theoretical result is a lifting theorem: QTT rank $r$ of the kernel implies matrix-product-operator (MPO) rank at most $2^d r$ for the corresponding convolution operator in $d$ dimensions, independent of grid resolution. This bound is sharp for our interleaved ordering. With quantics tensor cross interpolation, the moment-to-local stage of a single-level fast multipole method becomes a precomputed tensor-network contraction with quasi-linear complexity, retaining Lagrangian flexibility for immersed bodies. Our PyTorch implementation (\texttt{DiffVortex}) is end-to-end differentiable, runs on GPUs, and handles $6.7\times10^{7}$ particles on a single device. We validate against reference vortex-method results for an impulsively started cylinder and exact and reference solutions for inviscid elliptical vortices. We also demonstrate two-dimensional flows past rigidly moving, multiple, and deforming bodies, including gradients propagated through the full time integration.

infographic.key_insight: DiffVortex compresses the Biot–Savart kernel rather than the flow state, combining tensor-network acceleration with Lagrangian flexibility for moving and deforming bodies.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Its differentiable GPU implementation enables large-scale incompressible-flow simulations and gradient propagation through body–flow dynamics.
method: Evolve vorticity with Lagrangian vortex particles and model immersed bodies using bound vortex sheets.
Use quantics tensor cross interpolation to precompute tensor-network contractions for the fast multipole moment-to-local stage.
Prove that kernel QTT rank r yields convolution MPO rank at most 2^d r, independent of grid resolution.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports up to 6.7×10^7 particles on one GPU, validation against cylinder and elliptical-vortex benchmarks, and demonstrations with rigid, multiple, and deforming bodies.
infographic.watch_item: Tensor-network efficiency depends on manageable kernel ranks; the abstract does not establish end-to-end logarithmic scaling or general three-dimensional performance.
infographic.paper_title: DiffVortex: A quantum-inspired fast solver for incompressible flows

title: CARS: a centerline-anchored attention surrogate for coronary blood flow on skeleton-generated lumen geometries
authors: Reza Akbarian Bafghi, Sukirt Thakur, Maziar Raissi
abstract: When the parameter of a PDE surrogate is the flow domain itself, the key/value set of an attention model must encode that domain. We present CARS (Coronary Artery Rapid Surrogate), a learned surrogate for the finite-volume solution map of the steady incompressible Navier-Stokes equations on coronary lumens built from image-derived centerlines. CARS maps a centerline with per-point lumen radius and a scalar inlet flow rate to pressure and velocity at arbitrary query points. The attention focal set is the case's own centerline, so geometry fusion costs $O(N n_f)$ rather than $O(N^2)$ in the number of evaluation points. Trained per territory on $2{,}700$ OpenFOAM solutions with synthetic focal lesions, CARS reaches relative $\ell_2$ errors of $0.120/0.149$ (pressure/velocity) on left-coronary and $0.063/0.119$ on right-coronary test sets, in $87$~ms per case against a solver wall-clock of $572$-$1{,}063$~s. It outperforms four parameter-matched neural operators, and accuracy saturates eightfold below the operating focal count. Fractional flow reserve derived from the predicted pressure matches the CFD label at Pearson $r = 0.941/0.993$ and reproduces the $\mathrm{FFR}\le 0.8$ decision in $97.7\%/96.3\%$ of held-out cases. The predicted velocity does not satisfy continuity closely enough for derived quantities, and the weights are territory-specific.

infographic.key_insight: CARS uses centerline-anchored attention to predict coronary pressure and velocity in 87 ms per case, versus 572–1,063 s for CFD.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The surrogate enables rapid estimation of coronary flow and pressure-derived fractional flow reserve (FFR) on skeleton-generated lumen geometries.
method: Inputs: image-derived centerline, per-point lumen radius, and scalar inlet flow rate.
Uses the case’s centerline as attention keys/values to predict pressure and velocity at arbitrary query points.
Geometry fusion scales as O(N n_f), rather than O(N²), for N query points and n_f centerline focal points.
infographic.evidence_signal: Trained per territory on 2,700 OpenFOAM solutions, CARS achieved left/right relative ℓ₂ errors of 0.120/0.063 for pressure and 0.149/0.119 for velocity, with 97.7%/96.3% agreement on held-out FFR ≤ 0.8 decisions.
infographic.watch_item: Predicted velocity is insufficiently continuity-consistent for derived quantities, and model weights are territory-specific.
infographic.paper_title: CARS: a centerline-anchored attention surrogate for coronary blood flow on skeleton-generated lumen geometries

title: Swarmlet: a GPU-resident reformulated vortex particle method for coupled multirotor aerodynamics and flight dynamics
authors: Wyatt James Horne
abstract: We present Swarmlet, a GPU solver for the unsteady aerodynamics and flight dynamics of one or many multirotor vehicles. The wake is a meshless, evolving-core vortex particle field in the reformulated (rVPM) large-eddy formulation, coupled to rotor models of three fidelities, six-degree-of-freedom vehicles and flight control. Particles carry a smooth core of compact support whose field outside four core radii is exactly the singular Biot-Savart field, so the multipole far field of the treecode carries no regularization error. The subfilter closure is a dynamic eddy viscosity on a fixed filter width, applied by core spreading with a Lagrangian exchange of its local excess under an explicit stability bound, and the strengths are relaxed by projection; global corrections make both the exchange and the relaxation conserve total vorticity and linear impulse. All rotor models shed connected bound circulation, the disks along the arcs swept in each step however long, so the wake receives the lift impulse. The solver agrees with direct summation to $5\times 10^{-7}$ and converges at third order in time. Without calibration, an actuator-line model that includes its own near sheet predicts the hover thrust of a DJI 9443 propeller within 2%. With calibrated section polars it reproduces a Crazyflie propeller's thrust and torque within 3.2% at three speeds and the near wake of a hovering quadrotor with relative $L^2$ differences of 0.08-0.21 against particle image velocimetry, while the wake keeps the delivered impulse. A closed-loop formation of 100 quadrotors, run at a coarser setting on one GPU, illustrates the coupled method at swarm scale.

infographic.key_insight: Swarmlet couples GPU-resident vortex-particle aerodynamics with multirotor flight dynamics and control, preserving wake impulse while scaling to a 100-quadrotor demonstration.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The solver supports coupled studies of rotor wakes, vehicle motion and control for individual multirotors and formations.
method: Meshless reformulated vortex particle LES with compact-support cores and a treecode far field free of regularization error.
Dynamic eddy viscosity, core spreading and strength relaxation with global vorticity and linear-impulse conservation corrections.
Three rotor-model fidelities coupled to six-degree-of-freedom vehicles and flight control, with connected circulation shedding.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports agreement with direct summation to 5×10⁻⁷, third-order time convergence, hover thrust within 2% without calibration, calibrated thrust and torque within 3.2%, and near-wake relative L² differences of 0.08–0.21 against PIV.
infographic.watch_item: The 100-quadrotor case uses a coarser setting and demonstrates coupled operation rather than validated swarm-scale wake accuracy.
infographic.paper_title: Swarmlet: a GPU-resident reformulated vortex particle method for coupled multirotor aerodynamics and flight dynamics

title: Tandem jets in crossflow: the enclosed-recirculation momentum exchange and the unsteady shear-layer dynamics
authors: Xunchen Liu
abstract: Twin tandem jets in crossflow are examined by 40\ kHz time-resolved particle image velocimetry (PIV) over nine spacing--velocity-ratio conditions ($L=2d$--$4d$, $r\approx3$--7; 68 twin cases, 11 single-jet records). The front jet is diluted: its trajectory lies below the single-jet reference, with a near-field segment up to 40\% shorter, and its velocity ratio falls to an effective value $r_{\mathrm{eff}}<r$, while the shielded rear jet rises above the reference. This paper identifies the carrier of that dilution and the unsteady dynamics that sustains it. The rear-jet blockage closes a gap recirculation whose reversed flow puts the two gap-side layers in the counter-current shear-layer configuration, the classical route to enhanced entrainment. The measured Reynolds stress and Prandtl mixing length show that the absolute exchange is nearly independent of the velocity ratio and exceeds the single-jet leeward zone like-for-like by up to $1.5\times$ (zone peak, across conditions) and $2.8\times$ (area-integrated) at $r\approx7$. The gain comes from an enlarged mixing scale rather than from a steeper shear, and the front-jet near-field shortening follows the absolute exchange transport rather than the twin/single enhancement ratio. The turbulent term exceeds the pressure term in eight of the nine conditions, and the flux budget reads the dilution as a limited mass addition plus a momentum loss to the crossflow; the evidence remains observational. The gap-side layers remain convectively unstable---DMD and SPOD find no growing mode within the resolvable band and record length---so the exchange is carried by convecting vortex trains rather than by a self-excited global mode.

infographic.key_insight: Rear-jet blockage encloses a recirculation zone that enhances momentum exchange through larger mixing scales, diluting the front jet while the shielded rear jet rises higher.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Tandem-jet designs should account for gap-driven momentum loss and shielding rather than assume that both jets follow isolated-jet trajectories.
method: 40 kHz time-resolved PIV across nine spacing–velocity-ratio conditions.
Reynolds-stress, mixing-length and flux-budget analysis.
DMD and SPOD to characterize unsteady shear-layer dynamics.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 68 twin-jet cases and 11 single-jet records, front-jet near-field length decreased by up to 40%, while gap exchange reached up to 2.8× the single-jet area-integrated value at r≈7.
infographic.watch_item: The mechanism remains observational; no growing mode was detected only within the resolvable frequency band and available record length.
infographic.paper_title: Tandem jets in crossflow: the enclosed-recirculation momentum exchange and the unsteady shear-layer dynamics

title: Extracting target-related flow structures using a time-lagged cross-correlation ranking criterion
authors: Xuran Bao, Zhongkun Jin
abstract: Structures with large global contributions to a flow field are not necessarily those that are most closely associated with a specified engineering observable. We propose a time-lagged cross-correlation (TCC) ranking criterion to extract target-related dynamical structures from a fixed modal expansion while preserving existing spatial modes and temporal coefficients. The criterion ranks mode groups by the mean squared norm of cross-responses between their flow contributions and the observable over a lag window. It is tested separately using dynamic mode decomposition (DMD) and proper orthogonal decomposition (POD). TCC-DMD analysis shows that TCC recovers three low-contribution target structures from a dominant background in a synthetic flow. The reconstruction error for the target subfield is 2.15\%. In the cylinder wake, different force observables select structures associated with the vortex-shedding fundamental, slow drag variations, and the second harmonic. In the cavity case, selected modes connect two main frequency bands of the target observable to distinct spatial amplitude and phase distributions. TCC-POD analysis shows that the criterion minimises the weighted truncation error of the correlation operator among equally sized subsets of the fixed orthogonal basis. A comparison with canonical correlation decomposition further reveals differences between fixed-direction selection and correlation-based basis construction in the spatial structure and retention of flow information. Lag aggregation can improve structure identification when zero-lag association is insufficient. The gains depend on the cross-response distribution and window selection. TCC separates target-related ranking from mode-set construction, enabling comparison of spatial structures associated with different observables within the same modal expansion.

infographic.key_insight: Time-lagged cross-correlation (TCC) ranks existing flow modes by their association with a target observable, revealing structures that global-contribution rankings can miss.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Engineers can identify flow structures associated with specific force signals while comparing different observables within the same modal expansion.
method: Start with a fixed DMD or POD expansion, preserving spatial modes and temporal coefficients.
Rank mode groups by the mean squared norm of their cross-responses with a target observable over a lag window.
Select target-related structures without constructing a new modal basis.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests recovered three low-contribution synthetic target structures with 2.15% target-subfield reconstruction error and identified observable-specific structures in cylinder-wake and cavity flows.
infographic.watch_item: Benefits from lag aggregation depend on the cross-response distribution and lag-window selection.
infographic.paper_title: Extracting target-related flow structures using a time-lagged cross-correlation ranking criterion

title: Extended-regularized lattice Boltzmann method
authors: Luís Orlando Emerich dos Santos, Diogo Nardelli Siebert
abstract: Regularized lattice Boltzmann methods improve numerical stability by projecting the nonequilibrium distribution onto its hydrodynamic second-order Hermite sector and filtering the remaining kinetic modes. We introduce a separate relaxation time for the complete complementary kinetic subspace. The resulting extended-regularized lattice Boltzmann method (E-RLBM) interpolates continuously between the Bhatnagar-Gross-Krook and regularized collision operators while retaining a two-rate implementation. A Chapman-Enskog expansion shows that the isothermal Navier-Stokes equations are recovered with kinematic viscosity $ν=c_s^2(τ-Δt/2)$, independently of the kinetic relaxation time $τ_{\rm nh}$, whereas $τ_{\rm nh}$ changes higher-order truncation errors. For linear transverse shear, its first effect is a fourth-derivative term whose coefficient depends on the direction of propagation relative to the lattice. This fourth-order coefficient is affine in $τ_{\rm nh}$. For linear shear on D2Q9 and $τ_{\rm nh}$ between $τ$ and $Δt$, it lies between the corresponding BGK and RLBM values in every propagation direction. Stability maps for the decaying Taylor-Green vortex and flow past a rectangular obstacle show that an appropriate kinetic relaxation substantially enlarges the stable parameter domain. In a Taylor-Green convergence test with consistent initialization, all three operators converge at second order, and their error differences follow the hyperviscous coefficient for diagonal shear waves: the E-RLBM error is about 6% above the BGK error and about 40% below the RLBM error; in a double shear layer at Re = 80000, the E-RLBM follows the RLBM convergence curve. The proposed collision operator therefore provides a low-cost means of controlling nonhydrodynamic modes without introducing a full multiple-relaxation-time basis.

infographic.key_insight: E-RLBM independently relaxes nonhydrodynamic modes, continuously bridging BGK and regularized collision operators without changing the Navier–Stokes viscosity.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The two-rate operator offers a low-cost way to improve lattice Boltzmann stability without implementing a full multiple-relaxation-time basis.
method: Separate the second-order hydrodynamic Hermite sector from the complementary kinetic subspace.
Assign a separate relaxation time to the kinetic subspace.
Use Chapman–Enskog analysis and flow benchmarks to assess accuracy and stability.
infographic.evidence_signal: Stability maps show enlarged stable domains; Taylor–Green tests show second-order convergence with E-RLBM error about 6% above BGK and 40% below RLBM, while a Re = 80000 double shear layer follows RLBM convergence.
infographic.watch_item: Kinetic relaxation changes direction-dependent fourth-order errors, so improved stability does not guarantee improved accuracy.
infographic.paper_title: Extended-regularized lattice Boltzmann method

title: Neural Operator Splitting for Fluid Dynamics in Complex Geometry
authors: Jianxiang Li, Xi Deng, Hong Chul Nam, Anima Anandkumar
abstract: Solving dynamical systems in complex and diverse geometries remains challenging for both numerical solvers and learning-based surrogate models. We propose Neural Operator Splitting, a framework for learning fluid dynamics while preserving the physical structure of fractional-step numerical schemes. Instead of learning the full-step evolution monolithically, we decompose each time step into physically interpretable steps, and learn each operator separately using intermediate states from the underlying numerical solver. Guided by the linearity properties of the fractional steps, we introduce a conditional-linear Fourier neural operator (CL-FNO) whose linear state mappings are modulated by nonlinear conditioning on inputs such as boundary geometry. We further introduce two complementary strategies, symmetry sampling and corrective cycling, to mitigate error accumulation during autoregressive rollout. Experiments on 2D and 3D fluid flows with varying geometries and initial conditions show that our full model reduces mean relative $L^2$ rollout error by 68\% in 2D and 40\% in 3D compared with a single full-step neural operator. At comparable error levels, neural-operator inference is approximately $10^3$ times faster per step than the Monte Carlo solver.

infographic.key_insight: Neural Operator Splitting learns physically interpretable fractional steps instead of full-step fluid evolution, reducing rollout error in complex geometries.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could accelerate repeated fluid simulations across varying geometries while retaining the structure of fractional-step numerical schemes.
method: Train separate neural operators on intermediate states from a numerical solver.
Use conditional-linear Fourier neural operators to preserve linear state mappings while conditioning nonlinearly on inputs such as geometry.
Apply symmetry sampling and corrective cycling to limit autoregressive error accumulation.
infographic.evidence_signal: In 2D and 3D flow experiments, the full model reduced mean relative L2 rollout error by 68% and 40%, respectively, versus a single full-step neural operator; inference was approximately 1,000× faster per step than the Monte Carlo solver at comparable error.
infographic.watch_item: Training requires solver-generated intermediate states, and the abstract does not establish generalization beyond the tested geometries and flow conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Neural Operator Splitting for Fluid Dynamics in Complex Geometry

title: Monocular 3D bubble reconstruction: DNS-informed ray tracing and deep learning
authors: Chaitanya S. Nayak, Faizaan Mohammed, Vivek Kumar, Shivam Prajapati, Suhas S. Jain, Cyrus K. Aidun
abstract: Bubble size, depth, and spatial distribution govern transport and uniformity in multiphase flows. A single shadowgraphic view cannot separate bubble diameter from focal-plane displacement, as image signatures depend on both, while multicamera systems add optical access, calibration, and cost. We develop a single-camera physics-guided framework combining direct numerical simulation (DNS), validated Monte Carlo ray tracing, preprocessing, and focus-conditioned multitask deep learning to recover three-dimensional bubble position and physical-equivalent diameter from two-dimensional shadowgraphs. DNS-resolved bubble label images rendered at multiple focal-plane settings. The ray tracer reproduces shadowgraphic signatures with errors below $3\%$ (intensity), $1\%$ (apparent size), $15\%$ (blur), $6\%$ (numerical aperture), and $4\%$ (edge-spread-function shape), running $\sim30\times$ faster than the CPU implementation. The dataset has $900$ frames and $87{,}728$ labeled instances, partitioned by DNS timestamp to prevent leakage and expanded to over $10^{5}$ crops by broad-depth controlled-density rendering. A multitask network predicts signed depth and diameter from crops and focal-plane coordinates, achieving $\sim97.6\%$ normalized depth accuracy on held-out data; a closed-loop DNS-to-image-to-reconstruction test of $180$ bubbles gives diameter error below $9.71\%$ ($\sim90.29\%$ accuracy). On experimental images at four radial planes ($142$--$971$ bubbles each), PDF overlap is $68\%$--$92\%$ and log-PDF correlation is $0.72$--$0.87$. At the focal reference plane ($11{,}679$ bubbles), overlap is $\sim86\%$, correlation is $0.93$, and full-distribution, $D_{99.8}$, and composite errors are below $7.7\%$, increasing with focal-plane distance and defining a recoverability limit. Without stereoscopic hardware, the framework offers a scalable diagnostic for dense bubbly flows.

infographic.key_insight: Physics-guided deep learning recovers 3D bubble positions and physical-equivalent diameters from single-camera shadowgraphs, addressing size–defocus ambiguity without stereoscopic hardware.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a scalable diagnostic for dense bubbly flows while reducing optical-access, calibration, and hardware demands.
method: Render DNS-resolved bubbles using validated Monte Carlo ray tracing at multiple focal-plane settings.
Preprocess images into bubble crops and split training and evaluation data by DNS timestamp to prevent leakage.
Predict signed depth and diameter with a multitask network conditioned on focal-plane coordinates.
infographic.evidence_signal: Using 900 frames and 87,728 labeled instances, the study reports ~97.6% normalized depth accuracy on held-out data, <9.71% diameter error in a 180-bubble closed-loop test, and 68–92% experimental diameter-PDF overlap.
infographic.watch_item: Reconstruction errors increase with distance from the focal plane, defining a recoverability limit that must guide deployment.
infographic.paper_title: Monocular 3D bubble reconstruction: DNS-informed ray tracing and deep learning

title: Anisotropic spin hydrodynamics in a magnetized medium: entropy-current formulation and minimal linear modes
authors: Yiwei Qiu, Duan She, Defu Hou
abstract: We formulate anisotropic relativistic spin hydrodynamics in a parity-even magnetized medium using an Israel--Stewart entropy-current construction. Treating the magnetic field at leading order in the gradient expansion reduces the rotational symmetry to $SO(2)$ and separates spin susceptibilities and dissipative transport into longitudinal, transverse, and mixed channels. A restricted quadratic entropy current yields transient equations for the retained dissipative stresses and spin fluxes. We analyze a minimal linear closure around an unpolarized homogeneous equilibrium, retaining dynamical magnetic-flux perturbations but no explicit spin-magnetization coupling; spin and magnetic fluctuations mix through the fluid variables. Infrared coefficient equations and ultraviolet characteristic expansions organize the magnetosonic and Alfvén-like spectra together with spectator spin-flux poles. The first-order truncation exhibits unstable boost-sector poles and superlinear large-wave-number branches, interpreted as diagnostics of the truncated equations rather than microscopic dispersion predictions. For the baseline parameters, finite relaxation times yield asymptotically linear propagation branches and finite relaxation poles, with no growing modes found on the sampled grid. The characteristic speeds depend nonmonotonically on spin transport and provide necessary light-cone diagnostics, without establishing general stability or strong hyperbolicity.

infographic.key_insight: Finite relaxation times regularize the tested anisotropic spin-hydrodynamic model, replacing problematic first-order behavior with asymptotically linear propagation and finite relaxation poles.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The formulation offers a framework for modeling coupled fluid, spin, and magnetic-flux dynamics while screening transport parameters for relativistic light-cone violations.
method: Use an Israel–Stewart entropy current to derive anisotropic transient equations in a magnetized medium.
Separate spin response and dissipation into longitudinal, transverse, and mixed channels.
Analyze minimal linear modes through infrared coefficient equations and ultraviolet characteristic expansions.
infographic.evidence_signal: For baseline parameters with finite relaxation times, no growing modes were found on the sampled grid, while the first-order truncation showed unstable boost-sector poles and superlinear large-wave-number branches.
infographic.watch_item: The minimal closure omits explicit spin–magnetization coupling, and sampled stability plus characteristic-speed checks do not establish general stability or strong hyperbolicity.
infographic.paper_title: Anisotropic spin hydrodynamics in a magnetized medium: entropy-current formulation and minimal linear modes

title: DeHNSSo-v2: A compressible, curvilinear, and efficient extension of the Delft Harmonic Navier-Stokes Solver
authors: Pietro Carlo Boldini, Yifu Chen, Marios Kotsonis
abstract: We present DeHNSSo-v2, a major update of DeHNSSo-v1 (Westerbeek et al., Comput. Phys. Commun. 302, 2024), the open-source Delft Harmonic Navier-Stokes Solver for nonlinear stability analysis of shear flows. The new release adds a compressible formulation on general two-dimensional body-fitted geometries, automatic grid generation, linear-cost sparse assembly, reusable per-mode factorizations, and Newton pseudo-arclength continuation for high-amplitude nonlinear solutions. The curvilinear formulation preserves the fourth-order accuracy of the discretization on strongly distorted grids, and the compressible solver is confirmed to reproduce DeHNSSo-v1 in the incompressible limit. Validation spans published benchmarks for linear instability of compressible flat-plate boundary layers from $\mathrm{Ma}=0.5$ to $\mathrm{Ma}=4.5$, nonlinear oblique-mode breakdown at $\mathrm{Ma}=1.6$, nonlinear swept-wing crossflow compared with direct numerical simulations, and linear Tollmien-Schlichting wave interaction with a modeled surface-embedded Helmholtz resonator compared with experimentally validated linearized Navier-Stokes simulations. On the nonlinear test cases of DeHNSSo-v1, the computational developments result in a speed-up of approximately one order of magnitude. By broadening the scope and reducing the cost of DeHNSSo-v1, DeHNSSo-v2 provides the boundary-layer-transition and flow-control community with an accessible tool for studying receptivity, nonlinear disturbance evolution, and instability interactions with complex surface geometry and metamaterials across compressibility regimes.

infographic.key_insight: DeHNSSo-v2 extends harmonic Navier–Stokes analysis to compressible flows over curved geometries while delivering approximately 10× speed-ups on DeHNSSo-v1 nonlinear test cases.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The open-source solver supports boundary-layer transition and flow-control studies involving nonlinear disturbances, complex surfaces, and metamaterials across compressibility regimes.
method: Compressible formulation on body-fitted 2D grids with automatic mesh generation and fourth-order spatial accuracy.
Linear-cost sparse assembly and reusable per-mode factorizations reduce computational cost.
Newton pseudo-arclength continuation tracks high-amplitude nonlinear solutions.
infographic.evidence_signal: Validation covers linear boundary-layer instability at Mach 0.5–4.5, nonlinear oblique-mode breakdown at Mach 1.6, swept-wing crossflow against DNS, and resonator–wave interaction against experimentally validated simulations.
infographic.watch_item: The reported speed-up is specific to DeHNSSo-v1 nonlinear benchmarks; performance on new geometries and harmonic resolutions requires verification.
infographic.paper_title: DeHNSSo-v2: A compressible, curvilinear, and efficient extension of the Delft Harmonic Navier-Stokes Solver

title: Predicting trigger in streak breakdown via Picard-Chebyshev approach in plane-Poiseuille flow
authors: Nobutaka Taniguchi, Aiko Yakeno
abstract: The evolution of finite-amplitude disturbances is critical in the prediction of laminar-to-turbulent transition. To analyze the transient growth of disturbances, Pralits et al. (J. Fluid Mechanics, 2015) proposed a weakly nonlinear optimal perturbation (WNLOP) analysis that accounts for the effect of mean-flow distortion on the fundamental wave. The present study formulates a WNLOP analysis via Picard--Chebyshev iteration for compressible parallel flows to predict streak breakdown. The formulation incorporates the non-modal amplification of disturbances and their nonlinear interactions for polychromatic waves, considering all the possible nonlinear interactions starting from a finite set of initial wavenumber components. The nonlinear interaction is tracked as a monotonically increasing set of wavenumber components; specifically, the first-order approximation recovers the linear disturbance equation, the third-order approximation corresponds to the amplitude equation of weakly nonlinear theory, and further iterations systematically approach DNS results in the weakly nonlinear regime. By applying the proposed formulation to a subcritical plane Poiseuille flow at Mach number $\mathrm{M}=0.3$ and Reynolds number $\mathrm{Re}=3000$, the proposed formulation demonstrates high predictive accuracy in comparison with DNS calculations and succeeds in identifying the optimal perturbation restricted to a planar wave that causes streak breakdown in full nonlinear simulation. The proposed method predicts the nonlinear interaction between the streak and the planar wave, which generates an oblique wave and subsequent harmonic waves characterized by an alternating streamwise vortex structure, whose amplitude determines whether further nonlinear interactions are induced to trigger the turbulent transition.

infographic.key_insight: Picard–Chebyshev weakly nonlinear analysis predicts streak-breakdown triggers by tracking how streak–planar-wave interactions generate oblique waves and harmonics.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could support transition prediction in channel flows by identifying finite-amplitude disturbances capable of triggering turbulence.
method: Formulate weakly nonlinear optimal perturbation analysis for compressible parallel flows using Picard–Chebyshev iteration.
Track non-modal amplification and nonlinear interactions across an expanding set of wavenumber components.
Recover linear dynamics at first order and weakly nonlinear amplitude dynamics at third order, with further iterations approaching DNS.
infographic.evidence_signal: For subcritical plane Poiseuille flow at Mach 0.3 and Reynolds number 3000, the abstract reports high agreement with DNS and identifies an optimal planar-wave perturbation that triggers streak breakdown in full nonlinear simulation.
infographic.watch_item: Demonstrated accuracy is limited to the reported flow conditions and weakly nonlinear regime; broader applicability requires validation.
infographic.paper_title: Predicting trigger in streak breakdown via Picard-Chebyshev approach in plane-Poiseuille flow

title: CuAD: Source-to-Source Automatic Differentiation of CUDA Kernels for Discrete Adjoints in Computational Fluid Dynamics
authors: Seunghyun Joo
abstract: Discrete adjoint methods give the sensitivities that aerodynamic design and data assimilation require, but they remain hard to obtain for flow solvers that run on graphics processors. This paper presents CuAD, a source-to-source automatic differentiation tool that reads CUDA kernels and writes their tangent and adjoint versions as ordinary CUDA source. Its reverse mode is organised around the GPU thread. It adopts the convention of CUDA kernels that inputs and outputs do not alias, recomputes intermediate values instead of storing them, differentiates pure accumulations without a tape and keeps any remaining tape in a fixed thread-local array. We evaluate CuAD on four kernels from simple flow models and on a two-dimensional Euler solver. All generated derivatives pass dot-product tests to round-off, and the adjoint kernels cost two to six times the primal kernels. On a Biot-Savart summation compiled by one compiler, the CuAD adjoint costs about four times the primal at every size, as does Enzyme when the source declares the absence of aliasing with __restrict__. On the unchanged source Enzyme caches the loop in the device heap and costs 9 to 240 times the primal, while the heap tape of Clad costs 60 to 4400 times the primal and fails beyond 8192 vortices. Exact Jacobians assembled from the generated tangents also matter for accuracy. In single precision, the adjoint gradient of a finite-difference Jacobian reaches errors of 45 to 75 per cent on a stiff Burgers problem and of $5\times10^{-4}$ to $4\times10^{-2}$ on a transonic airfoil, whereas the generated Jacobian keeps them below $5\times10^{-5}$ and $3\times10^{-6}$. The applications include the shape sensitivities of lift and drag of a transonic NACA 0012, for which the residual, the boundary conditions and the wall force are differentiated by CuAD and the adjoint agrees with the tangent to $10^{-13}$.

infographic.key_insight: CuAD transforms CUDA kernels into tangent and adjoint CUDA code, enabling accurate discrete-adjoint sensitivities for GPU-based flow solvers.
infographic.engineering_relevance: GPU-native derivatives support aerodynamic shape optimization and data assimilation while avoiding finite-difference Jacobian errors.
method: Generate tangent and adjoint kernels through source-to-source automatic differentiation.
Organize reverse mode by GPU thread, recomputing intermediates and differentiating pure accumulations without a tape.
Assume non-aliasing inputs and outputs; store any remaining tape in fixed thread-local arrays.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across four flow-model kernels and a 2D Euler solver, derivatives passed dot-product tests to round-off, adjoint kernels cost 2–6× the primal, and transonic NACA 0012 adjoint sensitivities agreed with tangents to 10⁻¹³.
infographic.watch_item: Application requires respecting the non-aliasing convention and checking fixed thread-local tape requirements for each kernel.
infographic.paper_title: CuAD: Source-to-Source Automatic Differentiation of CUDA Kernels for Discrete Adjoints in Computational Fluid Dynamics

title: Spatially developing drag reduction across a finite oscillating wall
authors: Marco Galli, Nicolò Scaiola, Ferdinand F. J. Schrijer, Fulvio Scarano
abstract: The spatial evolution of a turbulent boundary layer at $Re_τ= 652$ developing across a finite spanwise oscillating wall is investigated with normalised oscillation period of $T^+ \approx 101$ and amplitude $A^+ \approx 7$, yielding a drag reduction of 32\%. The spatial distribution of skin friction is estimated adopting a recently introduced near-wall data nonlinear regression method based on the arctangent function, which circumvents the requirement of high wall-normal resolution to capture the viscous sublayer. The method viability is assessed against reference DNS data, and the trends of measurement errors from experimental data are well reproduced. The local impact of the control action is examined by evaluating the spatial development of scalar fields of turbulence statistics as well as conditional quadrant analysis to link the onset and recovery transients to turbulence events. The boundary layer response is observed to follow an exponential decay law for the skin friction spatial evolution. The decay length-scale corresponds to $0.6$ boundary layer thicknesses $δ$ for the onset transient and $0.9δ$ for the recovery one. The same exponential fit applied to the Reynolds stresses yields a response within $0.5δ$, with the exception of the shear stress peak, that requires a significantly longer distance.

infographic.key_insight: A finite spanwise-oscillating wall reduces turbulent boundary-layer drag by 32%, with skin-friction onset and recovery decay lengths of 0.6δ and 0.9δ, respectively.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These spatial response scales can inform the placement and length of finite wall-actuation sections for turbulent drag control.
method: Investigate a turbulent boundary layer at Reτ = 652 with wall oscillations at T+ ≈ 101 and A+ ≈ 7.
Estimate local skin friction using arctangent-based nonlinear regression of near-wall data.
Track turbulence statistics and conditional quadrant events across actuation onset and recovery.
infographic.evidence_signal: The skin-friction method was assessed against reference DNS data and reproduced experimental measurement-error trends; exponential fits captured spatial response scales.
infographic.watch_item: The reported drag reduction is not a net energy-saving measure; wall-actuation power must also be assessed.
infographic.paper_title: Spatially developing drag reduction across a finite oscillating wall

title: A second-order linear decoupled scheme with a relaxed zero-energy variable for Rayleigh-Bénard convection
authors: Matthew McCurdy
abstract: We construct a second-order, linear, and fully decoupled scheme for Rayleigh--Bénard convection between Navier-slip walls. The nonlinear terms are treated explicitly and multiplied by a scalar with exact value $1$ and no energy contributed to the continuous problem. As a result, each BDF2 step, with a rotational pressure correction, solves only constant-coefficient linear problems. For the time discretization, we prove that, for any time-step, the energy decays when the walls have equal temperatures, under a condition on the thermal weight, and the energy is bounded on finite time intervals when heated from below. Relaxing the scalar towards $1$ preserves both estimates. Energy stability does not control the accuracy of the scalar; the velocity and temperature fields are computed with its unrelaxed value, whose deviation from $1$ scales like $(E/C)(δt/τ)^3$ for kinetic energy $E$, time-scale $τ$ of the flow, and weight $C$ of the scalar equation. In our tests, choosing $C$ comparable to $E$ keeps this deviation small and doubles the largest time-step for which steady rolls are reproduced to a relative difference of $10^{-8}$. With Taylor--Hood elements, we observe second-order convergence in time, recover the critical Rayleigh numbers, and match published Nusselt numbers to within $0.5\%$. A three-dimensional implementation passes corresponding validation tests.

infographic.key_insight: A second-order, linear, fully decoupled scheme uses a relaxed zero-energy scalar to obtain energy estimates for Rayleigh–Bénard convection while requiring only constant-coefficient linear solves.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The scheme simplifies time stepping for buoyancy-driven heat-transfer simulations between Navier-slip walls without coupling the velocity, pressure, and temperature solves.
method: Combine BDF2 time stepping with rotational pressure correction.
Treat nonlinear terms explicitly, multiplied by an auxiliary scalar whose exact value is 1.
Relax the scalar toward 1 while preserving the proved energy estimates.
infographic.evidence_signal: Taylor–Hood tests show second-order temporal convergence, recover critical Rayleigh numbers, and match published Nusselt numbers within 0.5%; a 3D implementation passes corresponding validation tests.
infographic.watch_item: Energy stability does not guarantee scalar accuracy: its unrelaxed value drives the fields, with deviation scaling as (E/C)(δt/τ)^3, so scalar weight and time step require care.
infographic.paper_title: A second-order linear decoupled scheme with a relaxed zero-energy variable for Rayleigh-Bénard convection
